```markdown
# skills/harness-a11y-gate/SKILL.md
---
name: harness-a11y-gate
description: Build an accessibility gate that fails the build if a component has a11y violations.
tags: [ai, accessibility, quality, guardrails]
---
The harness-a11y-gate exercise builds an automated accessibility gate that runs on every PR. It uses `vitest-axe` to check for common a11y violations (missing alt text, low contrast, missing roles) and fails the test if any are found. This ensures that accessibility is treated as a hard requirement, not an afterthought.

## What you'll build
- A test file that imports `axe` from `vitest-axe`.
- A test that renders a component and checks for violations.
- A CI step that runs the a11y gate on every PR.

## How it works
1. Import `axe` from `vitest-axe`.
2. Render the component under test.
3. Run `axe(container)` and assert `toHaveNoViolations()`.
4. Add the test to your CI pipeline so it runs on every PR.

## Why it matters
Automated checks catch the mechanical half of accessibility issues. The experiential half (focus flow, keyboard operation) must be designed in, but the mechanical half (alt text, contrast, roles) should be enforced by a gate so it never regresses. This exercise builds the automated floor that keeps the site accessible.
```

```markdown
# skills/accessible-combobox/SKILL.md
---
name: accessible-combobox
description: Build an accessible combobox component with proper labeling, grouping, and error handling.
tags: [ui, accessibility, forms, aria]
---
The accessible-combobox exercise builds a reusable combobox component that is fully accessible. It demonstrates how to wire labels to inputs, group related fields, and announce errors so a screen reader user can complete the task.

## What you'll build
- A combobox component with a trigger button and a dropdown list.
- Proper `aria-*` attributes to connect the trigger, list, and error messages.
- Keyboard navigation to move between options and select one.
- Error handling that announces validation messages to the screen reader.

## How it works
1. Create a trigger button that toggles the dropdown list.
2. Create a dropdown list with radio buttons for each option.
3. Wire the trigger to the list using `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`.
4. Wire the list items to the trigger using `aria-selected`.
5. Add error handling that announces validation messages using `aria-describedby` and `role="alert"`.

## Why it matters
Forms are where accessibility often fails. The accessible-combobox exercise builds the three wires of form accessibility: label-for-id, fieldset grouping, and error-describedby. It ensures that every input has a label, related fields are grouped, and errors are announced to screen readers. This is the difference between a form anyone can complete and one that silently strands a screen-reader user.
```

```markdown
# skills/form-field-molecule/SKILL.md
---
name: form-field-molecule
description: Build a reusable, accessible form field molecule with labels, validation, and error handling.
tags: [ui, accessibility, forms, aria]
---
The form-field-molecule exercise builds a reusable, accessible form field that includes a label, input, and error message. It demonstrates how to wire labels to inputs, group related fields, and announce errors so a screen reader user can complete the task.

## What you'll build
- A form field component with a label, input, and error message.
- Proper `aria-*` attributes to connect the label, input, and error message.
- Validation logic that updates the error message based on input value.
- Error handling that announces validation messages to the screen reader.

## How it works
1. Create a label that is programmatically tied to the input using `for` and `id`.
2. Create an input that has `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` set to the error message.
3. Create an error message that has `role="alert"` so it is announced immediately when it appears.
4. Wire the validation logic to update the error message and `aria-invalid` based on input value.

## Why it matters
Forms are where accessibility often fails. The form-field-molecule exercise builds the three wires of form accessibility: label-for-id, fieldset grouping, and error-describedby. It ensures that every input has a label, related fields are grouped, and errors are announced to screen readers. This is the difference between a form anyone can complete and one that silently strands a screen-reader user.
```
